preamble: Deaffrication of the retroflex ejective affricate [ʈʂʼ] to the alveolo-palatal ejective fricative [ɕʼ] in Standard Kabardian (East Circassian). Where literary Adyghe (West Circassian) has чӏ, rendered [t͡ʂʼ] in Wiktionary's Proto-Circassian reconstructions and its entry чӏы [t͡ʂʼə] 'ground' and [ʈ͡ʂʼ] in Wikipedia's Adyghe phonology article, literary Kabardian has щӏ [ɕʼ]: Adyghe гъучӏы : Kabardian гъущӏ [ʁʷəɕʼ] 'iron'. Wiktionary reconstructs Proto-Circassian *t͡ʂʼə 'ground', *ʁʷət͡ʂʼə 'iron' and *qʷānt͡ʂʼa 'jackdaw' with the affricate and gives Besleney Kabardian гъучӏ (ʁʷət͡ʂʼ) 'iron', so the change is not shared by all of East Circassian. Wikipedia's Proto-Circassian article treats it as part of the same spirantization that turned *t͡ʃʼ into ɕʼ, so that in Standard Kabardian the two ejective affricates fell together as щӏ; it lists Bzhedug, Chemguy (Temirgoy) and Besleney as keeping [t͡ʂʼ]. Nikolayev & Starostin (1994: 199) likewise reconstruct two Proto-Adyghe-Kabardian glottalized affricates, *č̣ and *č̣́, that stay affricates in Bzhedug and Temirgoy Adyghe and both appear as ṣ́ in Kabardian. They do not call *č̣ retroflex, but in the words cited here it is the sound written чӏ in Adyghe, as the Starling entry for 'iron' (Adyghe ʁʷǝč̣ǝ, Kabardian ʁʷǝṣ́, Proto-Adyghe-Kabardian *ʁʷǝč̣ǝ́) shows. Wikipedia's Proto-Circassian article also lists the Abzakh dialect of Adyghe as affected, but the sources disagree on the Abzakh outcome: the article's correspondence table gives ɕʼ or [ʔʲ], its example table gives шӏ (гъушӏы 'iron', шӏыпӏэ 'area'), and Wiktionary gives Abzakh гъушӏы (ʁʷəʃʼə) 'iron' but щӏыгу 'earth'. In the Shapsug and Natukhai dialects of Adyghe the same sound merged with [t͡ʃʼ] instead. Several commonly cited pairs contain the morpheme чӏы 'ground' (чӏыгу 'earth', чӏылъэ 'land', чӏыпӏэ 'place') and are counted here as one example. In the Adyghe word for 'cold', чъыӏэ [t͡ʂəʔa], the affricate is not ejective.

examples.note: Wiktionary. Starling: Proto-Adyghe-Kabardian *č̣ǝ 'earth', Adyghe č̣ǝ, Kabardian ṣ́ǝ. The same morpheme is in Proto-Circassian *t͡ʂʼəgʷə 'earth' (Adyghe чӏыгу : Kabardian щӏыгу) and *t͡ʂʼəɬa 'land' (Adyghe чӏылъэ : Kabardian щӏылъэ), and in Adyghe чӏыпӏэ 'place', which Wiktionary derives from чӏы + пӏэ (Kabardian щӏыпӏэ in Wikipedia's Proto-Circassian article).

Wiktionary, which gives Besleney Kabardian гъучӏ (ʁʷət͡ʂʼ) with the affricate kept; the Adyghe–Kabardian pair is also in Wikipedia's Circassian languages article. Starling: Adyghe ʁʷǝč̣ǝ, Kabardian ʁʷǝṣ́. Starling reports that Yakovlev and Shagirov analysed the word as 'dried (ʁʷǝ-) earth (č̣ǝ)', which would make it share a morpheme with 'ground'; Nikolayev & Starostin reject this as a folk etymology.
Wiktionary. Wikipedia's Shapsug dialect article gives the same correspondence, Standard Adyghe [qʷaːnʈʂʼa] : Kabardian [qʷaːnɕʼa] 'daw'.

Starling, in the comment to its entry 'bottom', gives Adyghe č̣a, Kabardian ṣ́a for this root and keeps it apart from the preverb *č̣́a- 'under'. Wikipedia's Shapsug dialect article gives Standard Adyghe [ʈʂʼa] : Kabardian [ɕʼa] 'bottom'. Adyghe чӏэ 'bottom' from Wiktionary.
Wikipedia (Shapsug dialect), which writes the Standard Adyghe form with its own notation чӏъ for [ʈʂʼ]. Wikipedia's Circassian languages article lists Adyghe упчӏэ : Kabardian упщӏэ 'question'.
